title: Big-O Complexity
tagline: A single letter that tells you whether your code runs in a millisecond or longer than the age of the universe.

sections.content:
Imagine you write a function to search a list of users. It works fine in development with 100 rows. Six months later, the database has 10 million rows, and that same function crawls to a halt. No hardware upgrade saved it — the algorithm itself was broken. **Big-O notation** is the vocabulary that lets you predict and communicate this kind of problem before it ships to production.

Every algorithm consumes two finite resources: **time** (operations) and **space** (memory). Big-O is the standard mathematical language for describing how those needs scale as the size of the input grows. It does not tell you exact milliseconds — that depends on hardware, language, compiler optimisations, and cache behaviour. What it tells you is the *shape* of the growth curve: does doubling the input double the work (linear), keep it nearly the same (logarithmic), or square it (quadratic)? That shape is what matters at production scale.

Big-O was introduced by the German mathematician Paul Bachmann in 1894 and popularised in algorithm analysis by Donald Knuth in the 1970s. It sits at the foundation of computer science education precisely because it gives engineers a hardware-independent, language-independent way to reason about efficiency. A function that is O(n²) is fundamentally worse than an O(n) function for large n — no constant-factor trick can change that asymptotic reality.

This chapter will build your intuition from the ground up: the formal definition, how to read and derive complexity from code, the full spectrum of common complexity classes with real worked examples, the critical distinctions between best, average, and worst case, amortised analysis, space complexity, and practical strategies for the interview and production code settings where this knowledge matters most.

sections.title: Finding a Name in a Phone Book
sections.content:
Suppose you are looking for 'Yamamoto' in a paper phone book of one million names sorted alphabetically. Consider four different strategies and what they reveal about algorithm design.

Strategy one: read every name from page one. In the worst case — Yamamoto is last — you make one million comparisons. This is **O(n)** linear search. Doable, but painful at scale.

Strategy two: open to the exact middle. Is Yamamoto alphabetically before or after the middle? Discard the losing half and repeat. After one step you have 500,000 names left; after two steps 250,000; after twenty steps you are down to one name. For one million entries, at most ~20 comparisons — **O(log n)** binary search. The book can grow tenfold to 10 million, and you only need 23 comparisons instead of 20. Extraordinary.

Strategy three: for every name you find, search the whole book again to find all their friends. That is **O(n²)** — a million people each requiring a million lookups: a trillion operations total. At a billion operations per second, that takes 1000 seconds — over 16 minutes for one query.

Strategy four: you happen to remember exactly which page Yamamoto is on. Zero comparisons, direct flip. That is **O(1)** constant time — like a hash map keyed on the name.

Notice what we are *not* measuring: the thickness of the paper, how fast you can turn pages, whether you are tired. Those are constants. Big-O formalises this by asking: 'what is the dominant term that controls how the operation count grows as n grows toward infinity?' and then dropping everything else — including constant multipliers — because they become irrelevant at large scale.

sections.title: The Formal Definition — and Why We Drop Constants
sections.content:
Formally, we say f(n) is **O(g(n))** if there exist constants c > 0 and n₀ > 0 such that for all n ≥ n₀:

f(n) ≤ c · g(n)

In plain English: beyond some threshold input size n₀, f(n) is always bounded above by c times g(n). The constant c absorbs all the hardware-specific, language-specific multipliers. We care only about the *function* g — the shape of the curve.

In practice this means two things. First, **drop constant multipliers**: `5n²` and `1000n²` are both O(n²), because the 5 or 1000 is absorbed into c. At n = 1,000,000, both grow like a trillion — the 5x or 1000x difference pales against the n² factor. Second, **drop lower-order terms**: `n² + n + 100` simplifies to O(n²) because as n grows large, the n and 100 terms become negligible compared to n².

Let us verify with real numbers. At n = 1000:
- n² = 1,000,000
- n = 1,000 (0.1% of n²)
- 100 = 100 (0.01% of n²)

At n = 1,000,000:
- n² = 10¹²
- n = 10⁶ (0.0001% of n²)

The lower-order terms evaporate. Big-O captures the dominant behaviour.

Big-O is an **upper bound** — it says 'grows no faster than'. There are sibling notations: **Ω (Omega)** for lower bounds ('grows at least as fast as') and **Θ (Theta)** for tight bounds (both upper and lower simultaneously). When engineers say 'merge sort is O(n log n)' they typically mean Θ(n log n) — both the upper and lower bound — but O is used informally because it is the most widely understood.

sections.title: Reading Complexity from Code — A Systematic Method
sections.content:
You can derive Big-O by following a small set of rules applied directly to code structure. Internalise these and you can analyse any function in seconds.

**Rule 1 — Sequential statements add.** If section A costs O(f) and section B costs O(g) and they run one after another, the total cost is O(f + g), which simplifies to O(max(f, g)).

**Rule 2 — Nested loops multiply.** A loop that runs n times containing a loop that also runs n times is O(n × n) = O(n²). A loop running n times containing a loop running m times is O(n × m). If the inner loop's bound depends on the outer variable (like a triangle pattern), sum the arithmetic series: 1 + 2 + 3 + … + n = n(n+1)/2 = O(n²).

**Rule 3 — Divide-and-conquer halving gives log n.** Any algorithm that repeatedly halves the problem space (binary search, balanced BST traversal) runs in O(log n) time. The base of the logarithm does not matter in Big-O because `log₂(n) = log₁₀(n) / log₁₀(2)` — changing the base just multiplies by a constant.

**Rule 4 — Recursive complexity uses the Master Theorem.** For divide-and-conquer recurrences of the form T(n) = aT(n/b) + O(nᵈ), the Master Theorem gives the solution. Merge sort: T(n) = 2T(n/2) + O(n) → a=2, b=2, d=1, and since a = b^d (2 = 2¹), the result is O(n log n).

**Rule 5 — Built-in operations have their own cost.** `Array.sort()` is O(n log n). `Array.indexOf()` is O(n). `Set.has()` and `Map.get()` are O(1) average. `String.concat` in a tight loop may be O(n²) due to repeated allocation (prefer array join). Knowing the cost of the library functions you call is as important as analysing your own loops.

A common trap: the loop looks like it runs n times, but the loop body calls a function that is itself O(n). The actual cost is O(n × n) = O(n²). Always analyse what is inside loops, not just how many times the loop iterates.

sections.label: Example
sections.explanation: The key insight in `hasDuplicateFast` is replacing the inner loop — an O(n) scan — with a Set lookup, which is O(1) average because hash tables compute the bucket position from the value directly. The trade-off is O(n) extra memory for the Set. This **time-space trade-off via a hash structure** is the single most common interview optimisation pattern. Binary search uses `>>> 1` (unsigned right shift) as the midpoint — it avoids integer overflow in languages where arithmetic can overflow, and it is worth recognising this idiom.

sections.title: The Full Spectrum — Every Complexity Class in Depth
sections.content:
Understanding each class deeply — not just its name — is what separates rote memorisation from genuine algorithmic thinking.

**O(1) — Constant time.** The operation takes the same time regardless of input size. Examples: array index access `arr[i]` (a pointer arithmetic calculation), hash map `get`/`set` (one hash computation + pointer follow), stack `push`/`pop`. Note that O(1) does not mean *fast* — it means *non-scaling*. A database query with 10,000 JOINs might technically be O(1) if n is fixed, but it is slow for different reasons.

**O(log n) — Logarithmic.** The algorithm halves (or divides by some constant factor) the problem at each step. At n = 1 billion, log₂(n) ≈ 30 — you need only 30 steps. Examples: binary search, operations on a balanced binary search tree (AVL, Red-Black), finding the highest set bit. This class is extremely powerful and often underappreciated by beginners who see 'log' and assume it is complicated.

**O(n) — Linear.** Must touch each element at least once. This is often the theoretical minimum for problems where the answer depends on all inputs (you cannot skip any element safely). Examples: finding a maximum, summing an array, linear search on unsorted data, filtering with `.filter()`. This is frequently the target to aim for.

**O(n log n) — Linearithmic.** Appears whenever you sort (comparison-based sorting is proven to require at least this many comparisons in the worst case by information-theoretic argument) or do a divide-and-conquer where each level does O(n) work over O(log n) levels. Examples: merge sort, heapsort, `Array.sort()`, many geometry algorithms. This is the best achievable for comparison-based sorting — you cannot do better without making assumptions about the data.

**O(n²) — Quadratic.** Usually signals nested loops over the same data. Manageable at n ≤ 10,000 (100 million operations) but unusable at n = 1 million (a trillion operations). Examples: bubble sort, insertion sort, selection sort, naive all-pairs distance computation, comparing every pair of strings. In interviews, seeing O(n²) should immediately trigger the question: 'can I sort first, or use a hash map to reduce this?'

**O(2^n) — Exponential.** Grows so fast that even n = 60 is beyond practical reach on today's hardware (2⁶⁰ ≈ 10¹⁸ operations). Appears in brute-force exploration of all subsets (power set), naive recursive Fibonacci (`fib(n) = fib(n-1) + fib(n-2)` with no memoisation), and many NP-complete problems. Dynamic programming and memoisation are the standard remedies — they transform exponential into polynomial by caching sub-problem results.

**O(n!) — Factorial.** Even more explosive than exponential. Appears in generating all permutations, brute-force travelling-salesman problem. n = 20 gives 20! ≈ 2.4 × 10¹⁸ — beyond any computer today. Heuristic or approximation algorithms are the only practical path.

sections.title: Best, Average, and Worst Case — Three Different Stories
sections.content:
Big-O notation describes a *function of n* — but which function depends on the specific input, not just its size. The same algorithm can have wildly different behaviour depending on the data it receives. This is why we distinguish three cases.

**Worst case** is the guarantee — the most operations the algorithm can ever take for any input of size n. This is usually what engineers mean when they quote a complexity. It is the safe assumption for capacity planning: if the worst case is acceptable, you are protected. Binary search is O(log n) worst case.

**Best case** is the floor — the minimum operations for the most favourable input. Binary search is O(1) best case: if the target happens to be at the exact middle position on the first guess, you are done immediately. Best case is rarely useful in practice but can matter when data has known structure (nearly sorted data exploited by TimSort).

**Average case** is what you typically observe with random or real-world input, computed as an expected value over the distribution of inputs. QuickSort is O(n log n) average case — with a random pivot, the partitions are usually reasonably balanced. But QuickSort is O(n²) worst case — a sorted array with a first-element pivot causes maximally unbalanced partitions every time.

This worst-case/average-case gap for QuickSort is real-world important. Many early libraries implemented QuickSort naively, and adversaries discovered that feeding sorted or nearly-sorted data could cause DoS (denial-of-service) attacks by making web server sort routines crawl. The fix: **randomised pivot selection** turns the worst case from deterministic to probabilistically negligible — an adversary cannot know which permutation will be the pivot.

Merge sort, by contrast, is O(n log n) in all three cases — it always divides evenly and always merges in linear time. The trade-off: it requires O(n) extra space, while QuickSort with in-place partitioning uses O(log n) space (call stack only). This is why real implementations (like JavaScript's V8 `Array.sort`) use **TimSort** — a hybrid that adapts to data patterns, getting best-case O(n) on already-sorted runs while maintaining O(n log n) worst-case.

sections.title: Amortised Analysis — Averaging Cost Over a Sequence
sections.content:
Some data structures have operations that are occasionally very expensive but rarely so. Quoting the worst-case cost of a single operation dramatically overstates the real cost. **Amortised analysis** is the technique for finding the true average cost per operation over a sequence of n operations.

The canonical example is a **dynamic array** — the structure behind JavaScript arrays, Python lists, and Java ArrayLists. Internally, a dynamic array maintains a buffer of allocated slots. When you `push` a new element:
- If a slot is available: write to `buffer[length]` and increment length. One step — O(1).
- If the buffer is full: allocate a new buffer **twice** the size, copy all n existing elements into it, then write the new element. That copy is O(n).

Naively, you might say 'push is O(n) worst case' and leave it there. But how often does this doubling happen? If you start with buffer size 1 and push n elements, the doublings happen at sizes 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, …, n/2, n. The copy costs at those moments are 1, 2, 4, 8, …, n/2, n — a geometric series summing to 2n. So the **total** cost of n pushes is O(n), which means the **average** cost per push is O(n)/n = **O(1) amortised**.

Think of it like a toll booth where you prepay. Each cheap push 'saves up' a token. When the expensive doubling happens, those saved tokens pay for it. No individual push is cheated; the cost is just smoothed out.

Amortised O(1) appears in many important structures:
- `Array.push` / `Array.pop` in dynamic arrays
- **Hash map rehashing**: similar doubling logic applies when the load factor exceeds a threshold
- **Splay trees**: individual operations can be O(n) but amortised O(log n)
- **Union-Find with path compression**: amortised nearly O(1) per operation

When you see 'amortised O(1)' in documentation, it means: run a million operations and the total cost is O(million). No single operation is guaranteed to be fast, but the average is.

sections.label: Example
sections.explanation: Merge sort is the textbook O(n log n) example: each level of recursion does O(n) total merge work, and there are O(log n) levels. The memoised Fibonacci is the canonical dynamic programming transformation: going from O(2^n) to O(n) by caching sub-problem results. The two-sum problem illustrates a recurring interview pattern — sort+two-pointers gives O(n log n), but a hash map gives O(n) at the cost of O(n) space.

sections.title: Space Complexity — The Other Half of the Equation
sections.content:
Every discussion of time complexity has an equally important parallel in **space complexity** — how much additional memory an algorithm allocates as a function of n. The notation is identical; only what we are counting changes.

**O(1) space** — constant, or *in-place*. The algorithm uses only a fixed number of extra variables regardless of input size. Bubble sort and QuickSort (with in-place partitioning) use O(1) extra space (ignoring the O(log n) call stack for QuickSort's recursion). In-place algorithms are valuable when memory is constrained.

**O(n) space** — linear. The algorithm allocates a structure proportional to the input. Merge sort requires an O(n) output array at each merge level. The memoised Fibonacci cache grows to size n. A Set-based duplicate detector stores up to n elements. This is the most common space trade-off: paying O(n) space to buy a dramatic time improvement.

**O(n²) space** — quadratic. Storing all pairs, an n×n matrix, or a full adjacency matrix for a dense graph. For n = 10,000, an n×n matrix of integers is 10⁸ × 4 bytes = 400 MB — often too large for practical use.

The **time-space trade-off** is one of the fundamental patterns in algorithm design: almost any time improvement can be bought by spending more memory (caching, pre-computation, hash tables), and almost any memory improvement comes at the cost of more time (recomputing instead of caching, in-place vs. output array). Understanding both dimensions allows you to reason about which resource is the bottleneck in a given context — a memory-constrained embedded system has different optimal choices than a batch processing server with 256 GB RAM.

One subtlety: **call stack depth** counts as space. A naive recursive function that recurses n times deep uses O(n) stack space, which can cause stack overflow for large n. This is why iterative solutions are often preferred for deep recursion — or tail-call optimisation is used where supported.

**Input space is typically not counted.** When we say an algorithm uses O(1) space, we mean O(1) *additional* space beyond the input. The input itself must exist in memory, but it is not charged to the algorithm.

sections.title: Common Misconceptions and Subtle Edge Cases
sections.content:
**'O(n) is always better than O(n²)' — not always true for small n.** Big-O ignores constants. An O(n²) algorithm with a tiny constant (like insertion sort on nearly-sorted data) can outperform an O(n log n) algorithm with large constant overhead (like merge sort) for small inputs. This is why TimSort switches to insertion sort for small subarrays. The crossover point where asymptotic complexity beats constant factors depends on the algorithm and hardware — typically somewhere around n = 10–50 for sorting.

**'Hash map lookup is O(1)' — with an important asterisk.** Hash map operations are O(1) *average* case, assuming a good hash function with few collisions. In the worst case — a pathological hash function or deliberate collision attack — all keys hash to the same bucket, and lookup degrades to O(n) (traversing a linked list of collisions). Production hash maps randomise the hash seed to prevent adversarial inputs from triggering worst-case behaviour.

**'My for loop runs n times, so it is O(n)' — check the body.** If the loop body calls `Array.indexOf()` (O(n) itself), `String.includes()` on a large string, or any other linear operation, the total is O(n × n) = O(n²). This is one of the most common sources of hidden quadratic complexity in real codebases.

**'Recursion is elegant but slow' — not always.** Recursion's time complexity depends entirely on how many unique sub-problems exist and how they are combined. A naive recursive Fibonacci is O(2^n) because it recomputes sub-problems. A memoised version is O(n). The recursive structure itself is not the bottleneck — the redundant computation is. With memoisation or dynamic programming, recursive solutions can be as efficient as iterative ones.

**'Sorting is always O(n log n)' — only if you are comparing elements.** Non-comparison sorts like **Counting Sort** (O(n + k) where k is the value range) and **Radix Sort** (O(d × n) where d is the number of digits) can sort faster than O(n log n) for restricted input types. The information-theoretic O(n log n) lower bound applies only when the only operation allowed is comparing pairs of elements.

**Historical context:** The O notation was introduced by German number theorist Paul Bachmann in his 1894 book *Die Analytische Zahlentheorie*. The matching Ω notation was introduced by Edmund Landau in 1909. These were originally pure mathematics tools for describing asymptotic behaviour of number-theoretic functions. Donald Knuth standardised their use in computer science in his 1976 paper *Big Omicron and Big Omega and Big Theta*, which defined the conventions still used today. Knuth also introduced the Θ notation to fill the gap between O (upper bound) and Ω (lower bound).

sections.label: Example
sections.explanation: The `hiddenQuadratic` function is a textbook real-world trap: the outer loop looks linear, but `Array.indexOf` scans the entire array for each element, making the actual complexity O(n²). The fix converts the array to a `Set` in one O(n) pass, then each lookup inside the loop is O(1). Spotting hidden O(n) calls inside loops is one of the most valuable code review skills.

sections.content: **Interview strategy — state complexity before writing code.** Say aloud: 'I think this will be O(n) time and O(n) space — let me verify as I write.' This signals algorithmic thinking from the start. Three questions to always ask: (1) Does each loop actually run n times, or does it terminate early? (2) Is there a hidden O(n) call inside a loop, like `indexOf` or `includes`? (3) Can I replace an inner loop with a hash set to drop from O(n²) to O(n)? When asked 'can you do better?', the two most common answers are: replace an inner linear scan with a hash structure, or sort the input first to enable binary search. Knowing O(n log n) is the lower bound for comparison-based sorting is a reliable signal of depth — and knowing *why* (information theory: n! possible orderings, log₂(n!) ≈ n log n bits of information required) is even better.

items: **Big-O is an upper bound on growth rate** — it describes how time or space scales with input size n, dropping constant coefficients and lower-order terms because they become irrelevant as n grows.
The hierarchy O(1) < O(log n) < O(n) < O(n log n) < O(n²) < O(2^n) < O(n!) represents qualitatively different scalability — no constant-factor optimisation can bridge one class to a better one.

**Read complexity from code structure**: sequential blocks add (take the dominant term), nested loops multiply, halving-loop patterns give log n. Always inspect the body of a loop for hidden O(n) calls.
Best, average, and worst case are distinct — QuickSort is O(n log n) average but O(n²) worst case. Randomised pivot selection makes the worst case probabilistically negligible.
**Amortised analysis** averages cost over a sequence — `Array.push` is O(1) amortised because expensive buffer-doubling copies are exponentially rare, making the total cost of n pushes O(n).
Space complexity uses identical notation — trading O(n) space (a hash set or cache) for O(n) → O(1) time savings is the canonical time-space trade-off and the most frequent interview optimisation.
O(n log n) is the **proven lower bound** for comparison-based sorting; non-comparison sorts like Counting Sort can break this barrier but require constraints on the input values.

quiz.question: What does Big-O notation primarily describe?
options: The exact number of milliseconds an algorithm takes on a given machine
How an algorithm's resource usage grows relative to input size n
Whether an algorithm produces the correct output
The number of lines of code in an algorithm
quiz.explanation: Big-O describes the growth rate of time or space as input size n increases — not absolute speed. It is hardware-independent and language-independent, capturing the shape of the scaling curve.

quiz.question: What is the simplified Big-O for the expression 8n² + 500n + 10000?
quiz.explanation: Big-O drops constant multipliers and lower-order terms. The dominant term is n² (it grows fastest as n increases), so the complexity is O(n²). The 8, 500n, and 10000 are all irrelevant at large n.

quiz.question: Binary search on a sorted array of n elements has which worst-case time complexity?
quiz.explanation: Binary search halves the search space with each comparison. Starting from n elements, at most log₂(n) iterations are needed. For n = 1,000,000 that is only ~20 comparisons.

quiz.question: You have a nested loop where both the outer and inner loops iterate n times with O(1) work per inner step. What is the total complexity?
quiz.explanation: The outer loop runs n times. For each of those n iterations, the inner loop also runs n times. The total operations are n × n = n². Nested loops over the same variable are the signature O(n²) pattern.

quiz.question: You replace an O(n²) duplicate-detection nested loop with a Set-based O(n) solution. What resource does the faster version trade away?
options: Correctness — hash sets can have false positives
Space — the Set stores up to n elements in memory
Time — Set operations are slower than array comparisons
Nothing — it is strictly better in every way
quiz.explanation: The Set-based approach uses O(n) extra memory to store the seen elements. This is the classic time-space trade-off: spending O(n) space buys a factor-of-n improvement in time, from O(n²) to O(n).

quiz.question: Which statement about comparison-based sorting is proven true by information theory?
options: O(n) comparison-based sorting is achievable for any input distribution
O(n log n) is the theoretical lower bound for comparison-based sorting
Bubble sort meets the optimal lower bound in the average case
O(log n) sorting is possible if the array is already partially sorted
quiz.explanation: Information theory shows that to determine the order of n elements, you must distinguish between n! possible orderings. This requires at least log₂(n!) ≈ n log n comparisons. No comparison-based sort can do better.

quiz.question: JavaScript's Array.push is described as O(1) amortised. Why is it not simply O(1) for every single call?
options: push() always copies the entire array to validate element types
Occasionally the internal buffer is full and must be doubled, requiring an O(n) copy of all elements
push() sorts the array after inserting each new element
push() performs an O(log n) binary search to find the insertion point
quiz.explanation: When the internal buffer is full, the dynamic array allocates a 2× buffer and copies all n current elements — that single push costs O(n). But doublings are exponentially rare; over n total pushes the copy cost sums to 2n, so the average cost per push is O(1) amortised.

quiz.question: QuickSort is O(n log n) average case but O(n²) worst case. What input typically triggers the worst case for a naive first-element pivot?
options: An array with all identical elements
An array with an odd number of elements
quiz.explanation: With a first-element pivot on a sorted array, every partition splits into sizes (0, n-1) — maximally unbalanced. This creates n recursive levels each doing O(n) work, giving O(n²) total. Randomised pivot selection makes this case probabilistically negligible.

quiz.question: A function contains: a single for-loop over n elements, and inside that loop a call to `Array.indexOf()`. What is the actual time complexity?
quiz.explanation: Array.indexOf() performs a linear scan — it is O(n). The outer loop runs n times, each time calling an O(n) operation. By the multiplication rule: n × n = O(n²). This hidden quadratic is one of the most common real-world performance bugs.

quiz.question: An algorithm creates an output array of length n and fills it with an O(n log n) loop. What is its space complexity?
quiz.explanation: Space complexity counts memory allocated, not operations. The output array of length n is O(n) space. The O(n log n) loop describes the time dimension; the loop variables themselves are O(1) extra space. Space and time complexities are measured independently.
